attributes.label: Hotter, drier summers
attributes.description: Meteorological drought (KNMI'23): higher evaporation, summer precipitation deficit, and lower river discharge.

attributes.label: Sea-level rise
attributes.description: Rising sea level (KNMI'23 scenarios); increases hydrostatic pressure of marine water on polders and estuaries.

attributes.label: Wetter winters
attributes.description: Increased winter precipitation, providing potential recharge volume if retained.

attributes.label: Rainwater lens  recharge in the low  polders
attributes.description: The rain that soaks in and refills the rainwater lenses of the low polders: mostly the winter's rain surplus, since in summer most of the rain evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). On Schouwen-Duiveland upward saline seepage keeps it within the clay top layer of the low polders, and tile drains carry much of it off during each rain; recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island).

attributes.label: Rainwater lens  thickness in the low  polders
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lenses on top of the saline groundwater in the island's low polders, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them: about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground). These lenses keep salt out of the root zone and reach only the crop on their own field. A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (Rainwater lens recharge in the low polders → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders).

attributes.label: Land subsidence
attributes.description: Peat oxidation and clay consolidation caused by low drainage levels, lowering the land surface relative to sea level.

attributes.label: Polder surface  elevation (NAP)
attributes.description: Physical land surface elevation of the polder (-1.5m to -3.5m NAP), lowered by subsidence. Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014, p. 15); near Zierikzee the water holds under 10 mg/l, mostly fine sand, and its salt marshes rise 3–10 mm a year (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004, pp. 14, 27), against 16–32 mm on young marshes along the Westerschelde (De Mesel et al., 2013).

attributes.label: Root zone salinity
attributes.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which washes the topsoil of well-drained soil free of salt in one winter and that of badly drained soil in two or three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155–158, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
attributes.description: The upward flow of salt groundwater from the sand below into the clay and peat top layer of the island's polders, in mm a day, which leaves through drains, ditches and evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3662). The higher water pressure at depth drives it in the low polders, where it keeps the rainwater lenses thin, mostly under 2 m, and the shallow groundwater brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10); below the lens its water holds 10 to 16 g of chloride a litre (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675), against about 16 to 17 g in North Sea water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Most of Duiveland gets salt seepage, most in its low parts near the Oosterschelde (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 27); in the western low polders it is strongest near the Grevelingen and the Oosterschelde (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The flow follows the water pressures, which change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Soil structure
attributes.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.

attributes.label: Upconing of salt  groundwater
attributes.description: Upward cone of the salt-freshwater interface beneath pumping irrigation wells as the freshwater lens thins.

attributes.label: Farmers' demand for  deep polder drainage
attributes.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels, so that their fields drain: dry enough in spring for heavy machinery to work them, which holding water back for dry times makes hard (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44), and free of water damage after heavy rain, which farmers in the island's western low polders often find a bigger problem than drought (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). They put it to the water board as it prepares its water level plans, which it does with interest groups such as farming, and in views on a draft (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17): on Duiveland's draft of 2021, four views feared that a raise the plan proposed to study would bring more flooding in extreme rain (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53). Within the year, so an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Fresh water supplied  to the island
attributes.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry. Rijkswaterstaat makes that distribution: in drought it divides the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes among the users through weirs, pumping stations and sluices, by the verdringingsreeks when there is too little for all, and the greater part of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply (Rijkswaterstaat, n.d.).

attributes.label: Freshwater  availability for crops
attributes.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: rain, the soil moisture and groundwater of the field above the lens, water farmers pump or have stored, and water supplied from outside, which reaches the island nowhere now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 8). A Stock: water held in the root zone and in storage carries over from day to day: the root zone's is a daily balance, what the day before left plus rain, irrigation and capillary rise, less what the crop uses and what drains below the roots (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 85). It fills and empties within the season.

attributes.label: Freshwater storage  measures
attributes.description: The fresh water a year that the measures in place on the island's farms keep, store or collect for the growing season. They work three ways (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 16–23, 53, for the island): in the low polders, controlled drainage, anti-salinisation drainage (Drains2Buffer) and weirs in ditches keep the thin rainwater lens against salt, the water staying in the field's own soil, where it cannot be pumped (pp. 33, 53); on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay, the creek-ridge infiltration system, the Freshmaker and underground storage under a clay layer infiltrate winter water to pump in summer (pp. 20–22, 38); and double drainage collects fresh drain water into a basin to irrigate from (pp. 23, 29, 32). An adaptive practice: measures to keep more fresh water in the ground as drought and salinisation increase (p. 4). The study found them not yet fitted to the island and too risky for many farms to invest in alone (pp. 4, 11). A Stock: a measure, once built, lasts 15 to 30 years (pp. 17–22, 34). The farm decides a measure; infiltrating water needs the water board's permit or a notification, a weir the neighbours' consent, and raising a ditch's level the water board's cooperation (pp. 26, 44–45). Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session. Beside the farms, Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy shape it: in a demonstration with the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality, double drainage was laid on two test plots at Kerkwerve and anti-salinisation drainage on one at Dreischor, on three of the island's farms (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2023), the EU's rural development programme paying half of the cost and the knowledge parties a part of it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b).
attributes.simplification: Counts the measures of three kinds as one quantity, the fresh water a year they keep, store or collect, each kind reaching crops by its own link out: to Winter rain drained away, to Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes, and to Freshwater availability for crops. It assumes every kind responds alike to the drivers into this element. Every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what it leaves out is that a rise in one kind need not be a rise in another, so the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary them apart.

attributes.label: Groundwater extraction  for irrigation
attributes.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. How much and from where is Pumping the water board allows. Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Objections to land-use  plans
attributes.description: The views and appeals against the plans for the island's water and land while a plan is pending, the water board's level plans among them, which can slow, change or stop it. On a level plan, the views come in the six weeks its draft lies open and are answered in the decision, and anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). No source read gives the routes for the other bodies' plans.

attributes.label: Winter rain drained  away
attributes.description: Rain in winter that field drains carry off instead of refilling the rainwater lens: in the low polders tile drains carry much of it off during each rain (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661–3662, 3673–3675, measured on the island). It follows each rain, within the year: an Auxiliary.

attributes.label: Crop yield
attributes.description: Physical yield per hectare of conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt. The island's arable farms grow potatoes, onions, sugar beet, cereals, grass seed and vegetables in rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30, 38, from the farms studied), and some in the low polders have stopped growing sown onions for the salt (p. 31). A season's harvest: an Auxiliary.
attributes.simplification: The current crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) are one yield per hectare. Each yields less with a larger water shortfall, worse soil structure or fields that cannot be worked in time, so every link into the yield keeps its sign for each crop and no loop through it changes. What one yield leaves out: the crops lose in different proportions (the yield response factors on Crop water shortfall → Crop yield), and farms can shift their rotation among them, as some in the low polders stopped growing sown onions for the salt.

attributes.label: Local processing  capacity for new crops
attributes.description: Plants and supply chains on or near the island that store, process or sell new salt-tolerant crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Salt-tolerant varieties on offer. No source read shows a new crop processed on the island. Sea vegetables are sorted and packed by hand by a grower and trader at Nieuw- en Sint Joosland, who sells to restaurants and supermarkets at home and abroad and works with a colleague from Schouwen-Duiveland (FreshPlaza, 2018), its company growing at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023). Dutch quinoa's chain is run from Wageningen by GreenFood50, which has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities (GreenFood50, n.d.), and a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a). Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.

attributes.label: Adoption of new  salt-tolerant crops
attributes.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that tolerate salt. The island's rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30), and no source read shows a new crop grown on the island. Elsewhere in Zeeland, most still experimental and small (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57): samphire and sea aster, irrigated with saline water on the edges of salt marshes at Emmadorp, Waterdunen and Wolphaarsdijk, labour intensive and seasonal, their sales low (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6); sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat, where a new company worked out how to grow them, in fields and greenhouses, and set up their supply chain (EU CAP Network, 2023). Quinoa grows to maturity on irrigation water of more than 250 mM NaCl (van Loo, 2023, p. 77) and is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine, but needs a fine seed bed and weed control set by its row distance (p. 75). Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them. A Stock: a field keeps its crop through the season, and farmers move fields to a new crop over years, as they come to see the damage over dry summers (Harvest lost to salt → Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops).

attributes.label: Agricultural land  value
attributes.description: The price unlet farmland on the island sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect to earn from it. A buyer bids at most what an extra hectare can earn back over the years of the investment (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 2), and the price is set for an important part by what expanding farms earn on extra hectares, their income and expectations combined with what they can borrow: scale enlargement and low interest rates hold it up, swings in what the land earns and limits on banks' financing of land press it down (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 1–3). So it has risen far faster than what the land earns on average, tenfold since 1970 against two to three times for net value added (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 1). Farmers bought 54% of the land traded in the Netherlands from 2012 to early 2023 and investors 9%, their segment among the most active in Zeeland, where just over 1.5% of the farmland changes hands in a year (Kuiper et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). Banks hold it as security for their loans (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 3). No source read gives the island's land prices.
attributes.simplification: A soil's structure enters the land's value only through what the land earns (Soil structure → Crop yield → Farm income → this element), the sign the same, since buyers price what they expect it to earn. What it leaves out: any value a buyer gives good soil beyond its income.

attributes.description: The part of a farm loan's interest that differs between clients: the specific premium a bank charges above the base rate, which banks also call the credit or risk premium. attributes.description: European banking regulations requiring stricter risk weighting on loans when climate/soil risks reduce collateral value. attributes.label: Dependence on  high-margin  salt-sensitive crops
attributes.description: The share of the rotation under the high-value cash crops salt harms most, seed and ware potatoes and sown onions (Root zone salinity → Harvest lost to salt). Potatoes are financially attractive and sensitive to the climate, the most important crop of Dutch arable farming (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 12): on specialised arable farms on clay they bring in 55% of the arable revenue, ware potatoes 32% and seed potatoes 23%, against 14% for onions and 11% for sugar beet (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 14). In Zeeland, a manager of the cooperative CZAV says, a farmer earns his money not with rotation crops but with onions, beets and potatoes (Economic Board Zeeland, 2023, p. 19). A field takes potatoes at most one year in three against soil disease, so a farm growing more of them rents or swaps land (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 4). The island's rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed; in its low polders, where the seepage pressure is high and the surface water salty all year, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions, and with more fresh water they would be open to more profitable crops (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30–31). In Zeeland the sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 in 2024 after dry summers, poor harvests and a lack of fresh water, which four in five arable farmers have no access to, while potatoes held at about 19,000 ha (De Vriend, 2024b). A Stock: the share holds through the season and shifts over years (Root zone salinity → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops).

attributes.label: Farm income
attributes.description: Farms' income from their crops: the revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus the costs they pay (rent, interest, the water board's levy, their own pumping) and depreciation, as Dutch farm accounts measure it (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), per hectare in a year. Dutch arable farms earned about 65,000 euro per unpaid labour unit on average over 2010–2016, spread widely: in 2016 a fifth had a negative income and as many earned more than 100,000 euro (pp. 21–22). In 2025 an estimated 60,000 euro, lower prices after good harvests in north-west Europe and beyond outweighing the yields (van der Meulen, 2025). No source read gives the island's farm incomes.

attributes.label: Farmers' capacity to  invest
attributes.description: What a farm can put into an investment: its savings, built up from what is left of its income after the household's spending and its payment obligations, repayments included, and the credit a bank will give it. A farm whose income is negative cannot reserve enough for investment (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25), and one short of cash first cuts maintenance and private spending or draws on its savings, then asks its bank to defer interest and repayments or for more credit (p. 28); banks judge more and more whether a farm's operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Dutch arable farms invest mostly in machines, implements and installations (p. 19), and irrigation systems cost relatively much to install, not always within a farmer's reach (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28).

attributes.label: Financial leverage
attributes.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm, and it differs widely between farms (p. 21). Farms that expanded recently have a lower solvency, about 70% on large arable farms in 2015 (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); farms that own little of their land gain little from a rising land price but owe much less (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26).

attributes.description: Hectares of the island's land under arable crops, the census's akkerbouw, conventional or salt-tolerant and fallow included, whoever owns it: 9,094 ha in 2025 against 11,395 ha in 2000, on farms whose main seat is on the island (CBS, 2026). The farms growing them halved over those years, from 402 to 200, so the hectares per farm rose from 28 to 45: land from a farm that stops mostly goes in parts to neighbouring farms that are expanding, which can pay the most for it (Luijt, 2007, p. 25, nationally). The fall in hectares is net, the census's farmland 906 ha smaller and its grass and forage crops 1,431 ha larger (CBS, 2026). It falls when the land's holder, present or next, stops growing arable crops on it; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

attributes.label: Crop water shortfall
attributes.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. What a crop needs, whatever the water's origin, is the water it uses when it has enough, its evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.

attributes.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Provincie Zeeland, the actor here as the only body shown acting on the island's route, had a pipeline explored after the farming sector pressed for one (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7); the study leaves open who pays and who would run it (p. 51), and no source read shows a decision. By law a project decision can come from the water board's executive, for its water tasks, the province's or a minister (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 5.44), and the water board may charge the farmland a supply project serves up to 100% more, once at least half of its owners have responded and two thirds of those are in favour (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122); it charges more for its supply projects on Tholen and Sint Philipsland and in the Reigersbergsche polder (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, arts. 5–6). IenW shapes it twice: its minister allots the Delta Fund, from which a freshwater region can claim 25% of a regional measure's cost, up to 50% for an innovative one or one carried out by several regions (Algemene Rekenkamer, 2026, p. 31); and the Delta Programme 2027, under the Delta Commissioner's direction and presented by the minister with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes that the south-west delta's areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, the region open to exploring small extensions of the supplied area that add evident value, are future-proof and keep the extra demand on the Volkerak-Zoommeer limited, the demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet not raised (Ministerie van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat et al., 2026, pp. 88–89).

attributes.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is: soil work done when the soil is too wet smears and compacts it and forms clods, and more rain in spring leaves fewer moments to do it (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from the Dutch cultivation guides, on potatoes). attributes.label: Polder drainage depth
attributes.description: How far below the surface the water board holds the ditch levels in the island's polders (the drooglegging), as its water level plans set them: Duiveland's plan sets a target level for each of its level areas, from 0.8 to 2.7 m below NAP, in most the summer level higher than the winter one, against nature's order, to prevent water damage in winter and drying in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 63–64). It moves from the winter level to the summer one in steps in March and April, as the weather and the farmers' soil work allow (p. 66). On a creek ridge studied for water storage the depth is over 1.5 m in winter in large parts (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). The depth holds until the board carries out a new plan: Duiveland's plan of 2021 replaced one from 1982 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 24), and the board checks each plan every three years and renews it at 17 years or once it no longer fits (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17), so a Stock. Where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board has done where there is peat (2025, p. 13).

attributes.label: Water board's plans to  raise ditch levels
attributes.description: The water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, from the draft until their levels take effect. The board matches its levels to the land's use and soil, its principle that the level follows the land use: arable land 80 to 120 cm below the surface by soil, permanent grassland 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29; 2025, pp. 5, 7), weighing flooding, drought, fresh water and groundwater (2021c, p. 19), subsidence (2025, pp. 13–14) and a change's costs against its benefits (2025, p. 12). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, where levels had been kept low to store extreme rain, to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (2021a, p. 69). The general board adopts each plan (2025, p. 18); of its 30 members, 26 represent the residents and two the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, appointed by ZLTO's board (Reglement voor het Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, arts. 6–7). attributes.label: Margin given up on  high-margin crops
attributes.description: On the hectares a farm moves from its high-margin current crops, potatoes and sown onions, to new salt-tolerant ones: what the current crop would earn without salt less what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1). What salt takes is Harvest lost to salt, so it is not counted here. Potatoes, beets, onions and field vegetables are the high-margin crops; the margin of protein crops is comparable to that of cereals and cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9); quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small, against costs of about €1,470 a hectare (Cloet et al., 2024, pp. 2–3). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276), and on Terschelling food grown on salt-affected soil costs more to produce than food grown with fresh water, the project relying on volunteers and, at its start, on subsidies (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 13, 16). attributes.label: Adoption of  salt-tolerant  varieties
attributes.description: Hectares under salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops (potato, onion), which use the same machines, storage and know-how. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against the variety they grow now. A Stock: a field keeps the variety sown in it for the season, so the hectares hold until farmers sow again.

attributes.label: Machines and storage  for the current crops
attributes.description: The machines a farm owns that suit only one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45) and the buildings, machines and paving for storing its potatoes and onions (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), a store for long keeping being a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5). Nationally about 1,500 of the 3,725 specialised arable farms growing ware potatoes still had potatoes in store on 1 April 2020, which takes a cooled store, by the report's estimate (p. 7). Machines are depreciated at 8.2% a year, installations at 10% and buildings at 3% (p. 13, from KWIN 2018): about 12, 10 and 33 years, if that is a constant share of the purchase price. Dutch arable farms invest mostly in machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). No source read counts them on the island, where one farmer interviewed names mechanisation among the reasons for adding land (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57).

attributes.label: Capital lost on  switching to new crops
attributes.description: What the machines, storage and know-how of a farm's current crops would stop earning if it moved fields to a crop that cannot use them, less what it can sell them for. A store's costs do not fall when the crops in it take a smaller part of the rotation: they are sunk and cannot be earned back (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and other paths need new technology and skills while the old may not yet be written off (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It differs by what the farm moves to. Quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine harvester (van Loo, 2023, p. 75); adding protein crops leaves buildings and machines as they were (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4), and a store stands idle only once nothing it can hold is grown. A salt-tolerant variety of a current crop is planted, lifted and stored as that crop is, so it loses little of it, which no source read states. No source read says what a used harvester or store would fetch.

attributes.description: What the island's farmers know about growing and selling new salt-tolerant crops, from their own fields, their neighbours' and advisers.

attributes.description: What farms invest in carrying on with their current crops: wells and irrigation, drains, new machines and storage.

attributes.label: Banks' risk assessment  of farm loans
attributes.description: The risk a bank sees in lending to an arable farm: above all whether its operations will earn enough, over the years of the loan, to meet all its financial obligations, then its solvency and its land and buildings as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19; Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 3–4). Because arable returns swing from year to year, banks count farm loans as riskier despite the land as security, and the Basel capital rules steer them further toward lending on profitability and liquidity rather than on the value of the collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47); financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven they often count as a risk (p. 6). Rabobank's provisions for expected credit losses carried an adjustment of 87 million euro for climate risk at the end of 2024, set by sector on five events, drought and water scarcity among them (Rabobank, 2025, pp. 246–247). No source read shows a bank weighing a plan that may change what the land can earn. A Stock: a bank's view of a farm holds until the bank revises it, and it weighs what the farm can earn over the longer term rather than in one year (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans).

attributes.description: New loans and refinancing that banks grant the island's arable farms in a year. attributes.label: World prices of  conventional crops
attributes.description: The prices of potatoes, onions and sugar beet on the markets the island's crops are sold on, which its farms cannot move: what carrying on is weighed against. They form in an international market by supply and demand (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018), set by the harvests of north-west Europe and beyond (van der Meulen, 2025; for potatoes, Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). The Netherlands was the world's largest onion exporter in 2016, and by a rough estimate about 80% of Dutch onions are processed in Zeeland (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018); onions are rarely sold under contract, so their price swings (Bogosavac, 2018). The potato processors export an estimated 80% of their frozen products, and buy 90 to 95% of their potatoes under contract or in a pool, the rest free (Janssens et al., 2020, pp. 1, 7), a contract's base price published each year for the four large processors (p. 11). No source read here gives how the beet price is set.

attributes.label: Farmers' trust in  government
attributes.description: How far the island's farmers expect the public bodies that plan for its water and land to keep their commitments (compensation, their say over their land). Trust is typically created slowly and can be destroyed in an instant, and once lost may take a long time to rebuild (Slovic, 1993, p. 677, from US students rating hypothetical events at a nuclear plant; Remkes, 2022, p. 19). No source read measures it on the island: in 2013, 141 farmers in the south-west Netherlands, 16 of the survey's 142 on Schouwen-Duiveland, averaged 2.64 on a seven-point scale of trust in their water board on drought (van Duinen et al., 2015, pp. 745–749), and one submission to the Province in 2021 says the island's farmers no longer trust the Province on fresh water (Lases, 2021, p. 2). From outside the island's scale comes national policy changed or dropped: plans announced and then changed, postponed or stopped, which the National Ombudsman, from interviews with 32 farmers across the country, concludes has left the government unreliable for them (Nationale ombudsman, 2026, pp. 8, 15, 40), and a gap of trust with 'The Hague' (Remkes, 2022, p. 13). Whether the island's farmers carry that over to the water board, the Province and the municipality, no source read shows: a question for the group model building session.

attributes.label: Expropriation of  farmland
attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that a public body takes in a year for a use its plan sets, with full compensation, by an order a court must confirm. The municipal council, the water board for its water tasks, the Provincial Council and the minister can each give the order (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.4), and only for a use an adopted plan allows, after a reasonable attempt to buy the land and with a start likely within three years (arts. 11.5–11.7, 11.11). On the island it has been used for a roundabout on the N59 (Besluit rotonde N59, 2020, p. 3) and in 2026 for a high-voltage station on a site then wholly in agricultural use (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026; Braat, 2023, blad 9); no source read shows it there for water or nature, for which the Province buys on a voluntary basis (Provincie Zeeland, Jaarstukken 2022, p. 4). Few cases reach a court, in the Krimpenerwaard 6 of 69 files (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10–11), since the threat mostly makes owners sell (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, section Context of the Study).

attributes.description: How strongly farmers hold on to their land beyond its money value: family land, growing up on it. Whether anything on the map moves it, at succession perhaps, is a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: Hectares of the island's farmland that Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland's land-use plan (its omgevingsplan, with the changes it drafts to it) designates for a use other than arable farming, such as nature, water storage, housing or recreation. attributes.label: Freshwater lens  thickness under creek  ridges and dunes
attributes.description: The thickness of the fresh groundwater under the island's sandy creek ridges and dunes, down to the middle of the mixing zone with the saline groundwater: 5 to 15 m under the creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island), reaching about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). The lens farmers pump: wells are allowed only in fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick (p. 26), and it reaches crops through those wells alone (pp. 20–22, 26, 38, 53); on the higher fields above it salt is no problem, the saline seepage there being weak (p. 31). A Stock: it grows and thins over years (Freshwater storage measures → this lens).

attributes.label: Pumping the water  board allows
attributes.description: The volume the island's farms may pump a year under Waterschap Scheldestromen's rules. Where: from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). How: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field. How much: at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year, set at what rain recharges so the fresh-salt boundary does not rise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b). Extractions rose in recent dry years, and the province and the water board talk of registering the volumes more precisely (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021); no source read shows the farms' pumping changing the rules, the 2026 revision keeping the cap. A Stock: a notified well pumps until the board forbids it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b).

attributes.description: What the island's farmers, their advisers and contractors know of how freshwater storage works on the island: how the soil and groundwater behave, and what a measure costs, risks and yields. The knowledge from the pilots has not yet been translated to the island's soil, water and farm conditions, which leaves much uncertainty about building a measure, its costs, its management, its risks and its gain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11), and local advisers and farmers understand too little of how the soil and groundwater system works (p. 12). It builds up as measures are built and monitored, so a Stock. Outside the island's farms, Deltares, KWR and Acacia Water shape it: in the project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water they drew up quickscan advice for 13 farmers and feasibility studies for groups of farms, and made methods, maps and tools available with which farmers and advisers can go on by themselves (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 9, 55). The EU co-funded that project (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-a) and paid half of a later one, of Acacia Water, Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve, three farms and the municipality, which demonstrated and monitored new drainage on the island for figures and guidelines on building, managing and maintaining it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b); Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy explained its yield and effect at the closing meeting (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2024).

attributes.description: Summer precipitation deficit and high evaporation reduce natural recharge.
Higher sea level increases hydrostatic pressure beneath dikes.
More winter precipitation increases potential infiltration into the soil.
Higher winter rainfall peaks are mostly discharged under conventional drainage.

Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673). So a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.

attributes.description: Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3662, 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). On Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water a measure keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and lies too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when most of the island's shortfall falls (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). attributes.description: Higher polder elevation reduces the hydraulic head difference driving upward saline seepage.

Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year in the top 10 cm of soil with calcium carbonate, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil, while soil without it is expected to recover more slowly (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–228, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay.
attributes.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure collapsing within the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.

attributes.description: Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, p. 233, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. Whether what soaks in reaches the lens or leaves through the drains is set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).

attributes.description: Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the permit (pp. 26, 45). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: A larger harvest per hectare raises income at a given price, the price being World prices of conventional crops. The + holds in full where only the island's yield falls, to salt or a local shortage of fresh water. A dry summer across north-west Europe also raises the price, since the harvests there set it: for potatoes, north-west Europe is one market, and their price was highest in the extremely dry 2018 (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). Then what a farm loses depends on how it sells: in 2018, higher prices could help onion growers make up for a harvest forecast 44% below the year before, while potato growers mostly held contracts at prices agreed in advance (NOS, 2018), some 80% of the crop at around nine cents a kilo while free-market potatoes reached 30 (DutchNews.nl, 2018); onions are rarely sold under such contracts (Bogosavac, 2018). On the island, a farm with its own stored water gains from the high prices of a dry year (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 36). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R6: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R6 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: With the same debt, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (p. 21). A high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (p. 19); the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value. It holds for the land a farm owns: farms owning little of it barely gain from a rising price (p. 26). Within the year: the farm accounts value the land each year (p. 13).

Potatoes and onions are planted and sown in spring, and their soil work must not be done when the soil is too wet, which smears and compacts it and keeps an onion seedbed from forming; a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, from the Dutch cultivation guides). So the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring, which holding water back makes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Within the year.

More income from the land raises what buyers bid for it, through what they expect an extra hectare to earn an expanding farm over the years of the investment rather than through last year's income (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 2; Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 2–3). The + holds beside drivers the island's farms cannot move: since 1970 the Dutch price has risen tenfold while net value added rose two- to threefold, carried by scale enlargement and falling interest rates (Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Across individual land transactions in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2011, the expected revenue from the land had a significant positive effect on the price, beside land regulations, the spatial environment and local market conditions (Boere, 2015, pp. 81, 98). Years: the price follows expected income, and its swings ran over years, falling by half in real terms in the late 1970s and by 30% between 1995 and 2005 (p. 2): a delay.

attributes.description: Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds Crop water demand, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: what crops need is no variable of its own, so a crop's own water need, new crops against the current ones, cannot enter; no source read shows whether the new crops need less.

attributes.description: Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the ditches are brackish to salt, and no water can be brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 26): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not irrigate, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland through the summer, and an arable farmer irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). attributes.description: A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the sooner the fields drain and dry after rain. By the water board's rules for its whole area, the drooglegging is set at an optimum for each use and soil, against both wet and drought damage (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); at half the design discharge it must keep a field's drains, laid at their optimal depth, all but above the ditch water (p. 8); and an area 10 cm or more short of its optimum counts as too wet (p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40), and the move from the winter to the summer level in spring follows the farmers' soil work (p. 66). By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). The only views against a raise, four on Duiveland's proposed study of one, gave as their reason the concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53); none of Schouwen's opposed the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Elsewhere in Zeeland a view did change the same board's plan: on the raise of a winter level in the Braakman, near Terneuzen, ZLTO objected for seven farmers that one party's gain should not harm another, and the plan of 2015 took a phased raise, its first step only once the field that suffers most has been acquired and its second within six years (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops are often less tolerant as they germinate (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that holds on the island's fields, its thresholds not measured there. Within the season.

In interviews across the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them, salt in a field was largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield hard to put down to salt alone, and the damage not yet significant enough to make it urgent; it would take more dry summers like 2018 (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216). Nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance of salt and the hand work they take (p. 221). In Zeeland most farmers still grow the common salt-sensitive crops (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and on the island the response a source shows is giving up a sensitive crop, sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31), not taking up a new one. Years, as farmers come to see the damage over dry summers: a delay.

What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description. Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what salt takes.

More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, so their investment went to those crops and their logistics do not suit minor ones such as pulses (Magrini et al., 2018), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and process (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): a delay.

The more of the rotation is potatoes and onions, the more a farm spends on what they need: in farm accounts across the Netherlands from 2014 to 2022 a larger share of ware potatoes, seed potatoes, onions and winter carrots goes with significantly higher costs that no crop is charged with, buildings and machines among them, and storing these crops takes a store (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 5, 11, 15). The differences lie mostly between farms, far less in how one farm changes over the years (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4): a farm buys only as a machine or a store falls due, about 12 years for a machine and 33 for a building (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 13). attributes.description: A farm with less equity against its debt is a riskier loan: a high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19), and more financing still requires a contribution of the farm's own (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3). Banks weigh it beside the farm's cash flow, which counts more and more (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Within the year: a bank judges it with each loan.

attributes.description: A plan that may change what the land can earn enters a bank's risk analysis before it is decided.

Banks lend less to farms they see as riskier: they have become more critical in lending, counting farm loans riskier despite the land as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47), and hold back on investments not yet proven to pay (p. 8); Dutch farms' bank loans have fallen slightly in recent years, partly through the stricter rules (p. 19). Rabobank, which finances about 85% of Dutch farmers, says that since 2012, in a riskier world, it has often limited the level of financing on farms, and that a farm should be able to bridge two bad years without the bank (Banken.nl, 2019). What the bank charges for the risk is Risk premium on farm loans. Within the year: a bank decides on a loan when it is asked.

attributes.description: A new loan adds to a farm's debt while its equity stays the same, so its debt rises relative to its assets and its solvency, equity as a percentage of total capital, falls (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Refinancing replaces a loan and adds no debt: the link counts the new money. Farms that expanded in recent years have a lower solvency (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); Dutch farmers under 45 had 68% in 2018 against 76% for those over 65, their higher long-term debt going partly with taking over the farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26); on dairy farms heavy investment and poor results together took five points off solvency between 2006 and 2015 (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2). The sign holds with the assets' value unchanged: the debt of Dutch arable farms rose 38% between 2010 and 2022, yet in 2022 it was 28% of their balance sheet, the smallest share in farming, as equity grows mainly through the rising value of the land (CBS, 2024). Less credit slows the debt's rise; the debt itself falls through repayments. Within the year: a loan is on the balance sheet once it is paid out.

attributes.description: A farm with high debt payments keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops to meet them.
Farms that cannot refinance sell up.
Highly leveraged farms are the ones sold in a forced sale or bankruptcy.
A farm with a successor stays with the family; one without is sold when its farmer retires.
Farmers attached to their land sell it later, often only when forced.
Expropriated land passes to the public body that takes it, after a legal procedure.
Land that changes hands leaves arable farming when its next holder does not farm it.

Where arable farming still pays, its holder, present or next, keeps the land arable, while what arable farming earns, not what other uses would bid, sets the land's price. A decade or more: land leaves arable use only when a holder gives it up, and just over 1.5% of Zeeland's farmland is sold in a year (Agricultural land value).

Arable land needs lower ditch levels than grassland or nature. By the water board's rules for its whole area, a water level plan starts from an optimal level for each use and soil, the farmland's derived from the optimal drain depths for farming: for arable farming and horticulture 120 cm below the surface on salt-marsh clay (schorgronden) with no sand within 1.2 m, down to 60 on peat, for permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 7, 19), and for nature 0 cm as a general starting point, its levels set with the site managers, as Duiveland's analysis applied them to its land-use map of 2018 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29). So the more hectares farmed as arable land, the more land whose farmers need low levels, in spring as their soil work allows (2021a, p. 66); how strongly they ask for them, no source read shows (Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). Within the year: the need goes with the land's use each season, while the land leaves arable use only as it changes hands (Arable land in the polders).

attributes.description: A farm that pays finds a successor more easily.

A draft plan that would leave a field with less drainage depth than its use needs gives its owner reason to expect the land to earn less and so be worth less, before any level changes, and owners concerned that a plan lowers their land's value object to it and ask to be compensated; what the level itself does once it takes effect runs, years later, through Polder drainage depth and Spring workability of the fields to Agricultural land value. Respondents to Friesland's peat meadow programme said the uncertainty it creates for a farm's future value lowers the value of land and buildings before the programme takes effect, the 'planological shadow' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 3, 31). In their views on draft level plans owners named that fall: in two peat polders, holding the water board liable or asking for a compensation scheme (Graas, 2021, pp. 5, 24), and calling a plan unacceptable because its burden fell on the farmers, in the value of their land and buildings among others (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, pp. 5, 16–17), and in the Tielerwaard, on a raise beside a Natura 2000 area, as already at issue once the buffer zone was set (Waterschap Rivierenland, 2019, p. 8). A water board compensates only damage beyond the normal societal risk, the rest staying, wholly or partly, with the owner (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 16; Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 14). Whether and how far land loses value the minister called unclear for the peat meadow areas, the question being whether the yield can stay the same or the farmer can earn a comparable income on the land another way (Minister van Landbouw, Natuur en Voedselkwaliteit, 2021, pp. 2–3). Measured elsewhere, in polders where the level change answers subsidence; it transfers as an owner's response to a plan that would leave a field too wet for its use, as in the Braakman near Terneuzen in 2015, where the island's own water board answered ZLTO, objecting for seven farmers, that some would be left with less than optimal drainage depth or with drains under water in winter, both naming damage, not the land's value (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). On the island the raises of 2021 were to limit drought damage and give the crops more moisture (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 69; 2021b, p. 53): no view on either plan, as the board summarises them, gave the land's value as a reason, the only ones against a raise naming flooding in extreme rain (2021a, p. 53), as farmers across the salinisation-prone provinces want their levels low against flooding and to work their fields with heavy machinery (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 217), and one submitter on each half asked about holding a higher level locally (2021a, p. 53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether a raise that leaves too little drainage depth would raise this concern on the island, no source read shows, nor objections on this ground to the other bodies' plans. Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so B9 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: Farmers who expect public bodies to keep their commitments object less. In views on draft water plans in peat areas, owners named unreliable government, a hidden agenda and agreements not kept beside their other grounds (Graas, 2021, p. 13; Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 6, 14, 85; Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 29). In experiments with Dutch students, on a national board advising on carbon dioxide storage, how trustworthy the decision maker seemed explained how far they accepted the decision (Terwel, 2009, pp. 77, 81), and in the United States distrust of risk managers goes with political activism (Slovic, 1993, pp. 675–676). Measured elsewhere; it transfers as an owner's response to a body that plans for their land, whatever the plan's reason. It holds while a farmer still acts on the distrust: a view in Friesland reports 'weinig vertrouwen en veel gelatenheid' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, p. 7), and one submission has a small group on the island, no longer trusting the Province, starting a pipeline plan of its own (Lases, 2021, p. 2). None of the views on the island's two level plans of 2021, as the board summarises them, named trust (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53; 2021b, pp. 7–8). Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).

attributes.description: Farmers attached to their land resist plans for it beyond what it is worth in money.

Hypothesis, with two mechanisms for the group model building session: the conflict over a plan itself may lower trust, and a plan delayed, changed or dropped after objections may teach farmers not to count on the next one. Farmers do name changing plans as a reason to distrust public bodies (Farmers' trust in government), but no source read shows a plan changed because of objections costing trust, and where a body takes up an objection those who objected may trust it more, so the sign is part of the question. Within the year once a plan changes: trust can be destroyed in an instant; its recovery, slower, is in the element.
attributes.simplification: Folds Plans changed or dropped. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes. It assumes that a plan changed after objections costs trust as a plan changed for other reasons does, which no source read shows. The public bodies' decisions on their plans stay drawn, on the links from Objections to land-use plans into Water board's plans to raise ditch levels and Farmland planned for other uses.

attributes.description: Land taken against its owner's wish lowers how far farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments, the more so where they do not count the purpose as a public interest and where voluntary purchase was promised. Of 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, in a process of 2015–2023 ending in expropriation for nature, most experienced it as negative and named an inequality of power; the municipal council had feared for trust between government and farming (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10, 15, 55). In interviews across the Netherlands, owners who did not count the plan as a public interest, nature development for one, were more often negative about expropriation in itself than those taken for roads (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, section Equal Treatment), and the chair of LTO held large-scale use against reliable government, farmers having been told that purchases would be voluntary (Neefjes, 2008, p. 3). It starts before any order, from the possibility of one (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 55). No source read measures trust before and after, or on the island, where the purposes used so far are a road and the grid, those owners accept most. A tenant may gain (Adviescommissie Natuurherstel Westerschelde, n.d., p. 11). Within the year: trust can be destroyed in an instant, its recovery, slower, is in the element (Slovic, 1993, p. 677).

attributes.description: Hypothesis: storing water is a long investment that a change of rules can strand, so the less farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments on water and land, the less they store. A question for the group model building session.

The board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where more than 10% of the area is too wet, 10 cm or more short of the optimum, the target level is to be lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved, and where less than 10% is, a raise is considered (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40). Years, so a delay: the test runs as a plan is prepared, which the board does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: By the water board's rules the level follows the land's use ("peil volgt functie"): the board adapts it to what an area needs (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 5), reading the use from the current land use and from the uses the municipality's land-use plan designates, with what is expected within about five years (p. 7). A plan starts from the optimal level for each use and soil, nature's set with the site managers (2021a, p. 29), and where nature and farmland share a level area on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and proposes linking the farm parcel to the neighbouring, lower area (2021a, p. 61). So the less land is farmed as arable land, the more reason for a raise, whoever asks. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: The saltier the field, the fewer of the crops most sensitive to salt a farm keeps: on low fields with strong saline seepage on the island, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Years, so a delay: salt in a field is largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield is hard to put down to it, and interviewees expected it to take more dry summers like 2018 to make salt urgent (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216, interviews in the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them).
attributes.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

attributes.description: With more fresh water a farm keeps or takes on the crops that need it: on the island's low polders, with more fresh water available the farmer is open to more profitable crops and a more varied rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30). In Zeeland the area of sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 ha in 2024, the article naming the dry summers, the poor harvests and the lack of fresh water, four in five arable farmers having none, as farmers preferred less risky crops, while elsewhere the area grew (De Vriend, 2024b, for Zeeland). Years, so a delay: farmers respond to the seasons they have had, and the fall ran over five years of dry summers.

attributes.description: The margin given up is net of what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better a new crop pays the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to it. Quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small (pp. 2–3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Banks look more and more at a farm's cash flow, whether its operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19): the bank judges whether the farmer can generate enough over the longer term for interest and repayment, the expected income being the limiting factor rather than the size of the farm (Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 3–4). Basel IV steers banks further toward profitability and liquidity rather than the value of collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). So the less a farm earns, the more risk its bank sees, for owner and tenant alike; for the Netherlands. Within the year.
